planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September-April. Reineckia spreads by creeping rhizomes and fills in steadily to form a dense, low mat within two to three growing seasons.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Reineckia is an East Asian relative of liriope and ophiopogon, forming low, grassy, glossy dark-green tufts that spread by rhizomes into a dense, weed-suppressing evergreen mat well suited to woodland edges and shaded ground under trees and shrubs. In late summer it sends up short spikes of small, fragrant, pale pink flowers close to the foliage, followed by red berries that add quiet interest without ever becoming showy or overwhelming. It is considerably less commonly planted in American gardens than liriope or mondo grass, but performs a nearly identical function as an easy-care shade groundcover and tolerates the same dry-shade, root-competitive conditions under mature trees. Variegated selections with cream-striped leaves are sometimes available and make a brighter accent in deep shade. Established plantings need only an occasional edge trim and division every several years to control spread; otherwise it is essentially maintenance-free.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring next to a sturdy arbor, fence, or trellis; silver vine is dioecious, so a male and female plant are both needed for fruit, though many gardeners grow it strictly for its cat-attracting foliage and stems rather than for the fruit.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun on a sturdy support, since this is a vigorous twining vine related to kiwifruit; silver vine is best known in the West as a potent feline attractant, with dried leaves, wood, and galls used in cat toys because most cats respond to its nepetalactol compounds even more strongly than to catnip. Left to grow, it produces heart-shaped leaves that often develop a distinctive silvery-white blaze in summer, small white fragrant flowers, and yellow-orange fruit on female vines pollinated by a male plant; the normal fruit is edible though mild and rarely prized, while galled fruit caused by a gall wasp has a long history of use in traditional Japanese medicine. Because the vine is very vigorous and twining, give it a sturdy arbor or fence well away from smaller plants it could overwhelm, and expect enthusiastic garden cats to rub, chew, and roll on any part of the plant they can reach, which can slow young vines' establishment.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring next to a sturdy arbor, pergola, or large fence, since this is an extremely vigorous climber grown mainly for its dramatic foliage and fall color rather than for fruit quality.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun on a strong, large-scale support, since this East Asian ornamental grape climbs vigorously by tendrils and can quickly cover an arbor, pergola, or old tree. It is grown chiefly for its huge, heart-shaped, deeply veined leaves, which can reach 10 inches or more across and turn spectacular shades of crimson, scarlet, and purple in autumn, rivaling any deciduous tree for fall color. Small, fragrant flowers in late spring are followed by clusters of small, dark purple grapes that are edible but seedy, tart, and generally considered better for jelly or wildlife forage than fresh eating. Because of its exceptional vigor, Crimson Glory Vine needs a sturdy, generously sized structure and room to run, and benefits from hard annual pruning in late winter to control size and encourage the largest, most colorful leaves the following season.
